titel: Gross, net and the marginal tax rate in the US
kurz: How federal income tax and payroll taxes, two deduction systems with opposite logic, lead from gross to net pay in the US, and why the marginal tax rate is decisive for almost every financial decision.

bloecke.md: Between the salary in your offer letter and the amount that arrives in your account lie two deduction systems that follow opposite rules. Federal income tax is progressive and open-ended at the top. The higher your taxable income, the higher the rate on the top slice of it. Payroll taxes for Social Security and Medicare (FICA), by contrast, are levied at a fixed percentage, and the Social Security part only up to a ceiling. With only one of the two rules in mind, you regularly reach wrong conclusions, for example that a raise can push you into a higher bracket and leave you with less money, or that top earners always hand over the largest percentage of every additional dollar.

## Structure of the federal income tax

The federal tax rates are set out in 26 U.S.C. § 1, and the IRS adjusts the bracket thresholds for inflation every year; the 2026 values were published in Rev. Proc. 2025-32. The tax base is [[Taxable income|taxable income]], not gross pay. Starting from your wages, pre-tax contributions such as traditional 401(k) deferrals and health premiums paid through your employer are already left out; other adjustments such as HSA contributions lead to adjusted gross income (AGI). From that you subtract either the **standard deduction** or your itemized deductions, whichever is larger.

In 2026, the standard deduction is $16,100 for single filers, $32,200 for married couples filing jointly and $24,150 for heads of household. Above it, the rate rises in seven steps from 10% to 37%. Each rate applies only to the slice of income within its bracket. For a single filer who takes the standard deduction, the 22% bracket begins at a gross income of $66,500 and the 24% bracket at $121,800. The 32% bracket starts at a taxable income of $201,775 and the top rate of 37% above $640,600.

For married couples filing jointly, the bracket thresholds are exactly twice the single thresholds up to and including the 32% bracket; only the 35% bracket ends at $768,700 instead of twice $640,600. A couple with one earner therefore usually pays less tax after marrying (marriage bonus), while a marriage penalty in the brackets arises only at very high incomes. On top of the federal tax come state and in some places local income taxes.

bloecke.md:
## Marginal tax rate and average tax rate

The [[Marginal tax rate|marginal tax rate]] shows how much tax is due on the next dollar earned. The [[Average tax rate|average tax rate]] shows what share of total income already goes in tax. Both figures relate to the same income and differ considerably.

For a single filer with a taxable income of $75,000, federal income tax for 2026 is $11,212. The average tax rate is therefore 15.0%, the marginal tax rate 22%. This difference follows from the basic idea of brackets. The higher rate applies only to the dollars above the threshold, never to the whole income. Moving into a higher bracket therefore never reduces take-home pay through the brackets themselves. Because the top federal rate is 37%, at least 63 cents of every additional dollar remain before payroll and state taxes. Exceptions, where more income can cost more than it brings, arise from benefits and credits that phase out with income (see below).

bloecke.unter: The marginal rate rises in steps, the average rate smoothly and always below it. Own calculation from the 2026 brackets, without state taxes, payroll taxes or credits.

bloecke.md: The average tax rate is useful for looking back, for example to assess last year's tax burden. For every decision about overtime, a side job, a donation, a retirement contribution or further training, only the marginal tax rate counts, because each of these decisions changes only the top slice of income.

## State and local income taxes

Most states levy their own income tax, some with a flat rate, others with brackets of their own. Nine states do not tax wages: Alaska, Florida, Nevada, New Hampshire, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Washington and Wyoming. Some cities and counties add a local income tax, New York City being the best-known example. State and local income taxes add directly to your marginal rate.

On the federal return, state and local taxes can only be deducted if you itemize, and together with property taxes only up to the SALT cap. The cap was raised substantially from 2025 for several years and is reduced again for high incomes. For the majority of households, which take the standard deduction, state income tax therefore brings no federal tax saving.

## Payroll taxes as the second deduction system

Payroll taxes under the Federal Insurance Contributions Act (FICA) finance Social Security and Medicare. They are matched by future entitlements to benefits, but in the net pay calculation they work like a tax. They differ from income tax in three respects. There is no standard deduction, so they apply from the first dollar of wages. The rate is proportional rather than progressive. And the Social Security part ends at a ceiling, the wage base. Unlike in some other countries, employees cannot deduct their share from taxable income.

bloecke.md:
The employer pays the same 6.2% and 1.45% again on top of your salary. Self-employed people pay both halves themselves as self-employment tax and may deduct half of it from income. If you work for several employers in one year and together they withhold Social Security tax on more than the wage base, you get the excess back as a credit on your tax return.

Above the wage base, no further Social Security tax is due. This has a consequence that is missing from most debates about progression. The *marginal burden*, meaning income tax and payroll tax combined on the next dollar, does not rise continuously with income. For a single filer it drops by 6.2 percentage points once wages exceed $184,500 and rises again by 0.9 points above $200,000. Not all pre-tax deductions work the same way either: health premiums paid through a cafeteria plan and HSA contributions through payroll reduce both income tax and FICA, while traditional 401(k) contributions reduce only income tax.

The calculation assumes a single filer with no children and no pre-tax deductions, who takes the standard deduction and lives in a state without income tax.

1. Payroll taxes are 7.65% of $75,000, that is, $5,737.50 (Social Security $4,650, Medicare $1,087.50). The wage base has not been reached.
2. Taxable income is $58,900, that is, $75,000 minus the standard deduction of $16,100.
3. Federal income tax is $7,670 (10% on $12,400, 12% on $38,000, 22% on $8,500). The average tax rate on taxable income is 13.0%, the marginal tax rate 22%.
4. Net pay is $61,592.50, around $5,133 a month. Total deductions amount to 17.9% of gross pay.

The marginal burden, which this list does not show, is more revealing. Of $1,000 more gross pay, $703.50 remains here; $76.50 goes to payroll taxes and $220 to the IRS. In a state with a 5% income tax, roughly another $50 would be due.

*Simplified illustrative calculation without state tax, credits such as the child tax credit, or retirement contributions. Withholding from each paycheck follows your Form W-4; what counts is the annual return on Form 1040.*

bloecke.md:
## The marginal tax rate and financial decisions

Every dollar that reduces taxable income saves tax at the marginal rate, not at the average rate. This applies to traditional 401(k) and IRA contributions, HSA contributions and, if you itemize, to deductions such as mortgage interest and donations. The catch: most households take the standard deduction, and for them additional itemizable expenses save nothing until their total exceeds the standard deduction. From 2026, people who do not itemize may deduct cash donations to charities of up to $1,000 ($2,000 for joint filers). A deductible donation of $1,000 costs $760 net at a marginal rate of 24%, but $880 at 12%.

Three conclusions follow from this. First, a traditional 401(k) or IRA, which reduces taxable income today and is taxed as income later, pays off precisely when the marginal rate in retirement turns out lower than today; if it will be higher, a Roth account is better. You should check this assumption rather than simply take it for granted. Second, long-term capital gains and qualified dividends are taxed at separate rates of 0%, 15% or 20%, which is an advantage over wages for most investors. Third, timing matters. If you bunch several years of donations into one year, for example through a donor-advised fund, you can exceed the standard deduction in that year and take it in the others.

Form W-4 does not change the amount of annual tax. It only determines how much is withheld from each paycheck. The final tax depends solely on the annual return. A large refund is an interest-free loan to the government; a large balance due can cost an underpayment penalty unless withholding and estimated payments cover at least 90% of this year's tax or 100% of last year's (110% if last year's AGI was above $150,000). Couples where both work and people with several jobs are particularly often underwithheld; the IRS Tax Withholding Estimator helps to set the form correctly.

Benefits and credits that phase out with income raise the effective marginal rate above the bracket rate. Examples are the earned income tax credit, ACA premium tax credits, the phase-out of the child tax credit, the taxation of Social Security benefits and income-based Medicare premiums. In a few ranges, a raise can even reduce total resources, for example when eligibility for Medicaid or another benefit ends abruptly. Anyone close to such a threshold should calculate before accepting additional income or making a Roth conversion.

- Work out your combined marginal rate once and remember it: federal bracket plus state rate plus 7.65% payroll tax up to the wage base. With it, almost every decision that costs or saves money can be converted into net amounts.
- Check your Form W-4 after every change: marriage, a child, a second job, a raise. The withholding estimator on irs.gov takes a few minutes.
- Use pre-tax benefits that also save payroll tax, above all an HSA through payroll if you have a high-deductible health plan.
- Calculate in marginal net amounts, but negotiate in gross. On every gross dollar, the employer pays 7.65% in payroll taxes on top, plus the cost of benefits.

bloecke.md:
For the single filer from the example with a taxable income of $58,900, the tax is calculated slice by slice:

`10% × 12,400 = 1,240`

`12% × (50,400 - 12,400) = 12% × 38,000 = 4,560`

`22% × (58,900 - 50,400) = 22% × 8,500 = 1,870`

Together that is $7,670. The marginal rate is the rate of the bracket in which the last dollar lies, here 22%.

If the same person were married to a partner without income and filed jointly, taxable income would be $75,000 minus $32,200 = $42,800. The tax would be 10% × 24,800 + 12% × 18,000 = 2,480 + 2,160 = $4,640, that is, $3,030 less. That is the marriage bonus for couples with one earner.

mitnehmen: Federal income tax rises in brackets and has no upper limit; payroll taxes are proportional, and the Social Security part ends at the wage base of $184,500 (2026).
The average tax rate describes the burden in retrospect; for every new decision, the marginal rate including state and payroll taxes is what counts.
Moving into a higher bracket never reduces take-home pay through the brackets themselves; only phase-outs of benefits and credits can do that.
Deductions save at the marginal rate only if you itemize; most households take the standard deduction of $16,100 (single) or $32,200 (joint) in 2026.
Form W-4 only shifts withholding during the year; the final settlement is always the annual return.

begriffe.text: Tax rate on the next additional dollar earned. In the US federal income tax it is the rate of the bracket in which the last dollar falls, between 10% and 37% in 2026; for a complete picture, state taxes and payroll taxes are added.
Total income tax divided by income. It is always lower than the marginal tax rate and only meaningful in retrospect. It is often called the effective tax rate.

Fixed amount that is subtracted from adjusted gross income if you do not itemize deductions. In 2026 it is $16,100 for single filers, $32,200 for married couples filing jointly and $24,150 for heads of household.

Payroll taxes under the Federal Insurance Contributions Act for Social Security (6.2%) and Medicare (1.45%), each paid by employee and employer. An Additional Medicare Tax of 0.9% applies to wages above $200,000 (single).
Annual wage ceiling up to which Social Security tax is levied. In 2026 it is $184,500. Medicare tax has no such ceiling.
Form with which employees tell their employer how much federal income tax to withhold from each paycheck. It changes only the timing of payments, not the annual tax.
